teaching.causalExplanation: These rules come from IUPAC, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, so chemists everywhere use the same names. The first step is always the same. Look at the elements. A metal with a non-metal, or the ammonium ion, means an ionic compound, made of ions. Only non-metals means a covalent compound, where the atoms share electrons instead. The two kinds are named in different ways. Start with the simplest ionic compounds, made of two elements. Name the metal first, unchanged. Then change the ending of the non-metal's name, so chlorine becomes chloride, oxygen becomes oxide, and sulfur becomes sulfide. So N a C l is sodium chloride, and M g O is magnesium oxide. Notice there are no numbers in these names. Sodium and magnesium each form only one ion, so the charges already fix the ratio. Quick prediction. What's the name of K two O, made from potassium and oxygen? Have a think.

- **Hook with real objects (site hook: Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺).** Two powders made only of copper and oxygen: red copper(I) oxide and black copper(II) oxide (new plates). "Copper oxide" cannot name both; this drives the Stock numeral.

- **Stock naming is the taught route; compositional names are valid (Revision 2, root decision 37).** The video teaches Stock names (copper(II) chloride) as the route students use. Compositional names that count ions with prefixes (copper dichloride, iron trichloride, dipotassium oxide) are valid IUPAC names and are never called wrong or crossed; scene 11 says students will see them in other books. Errors crossed in this video are genuine slips only: an ambiguous name with no charge ("copper chloride"), a wrong charge ("iron(II) sulfate" for Fe₂(SO₄)₃), a wrong ion ("sodium sulfide" for Na₂SO₄) or a covalent name that does not count ("sulfur oxide").
- **Stock numeral as charge (route stop: "the numeral gives oxidation state rather than atom count").** "Oxidation state" is named once as the term for that charge; the definition stays "the charge on the metal ion" (author note b).
- **Covalent prefixes with the cause.** Non-metals form no ions, so no charges fix the ratio; carbon and oxygen make both CO and CO₂, so the name must count atoms. Prefixes mono to hexa (site lists to tetra; penta and hexa added for PCl₅ and SF₆). Vowel dropping named only through "monoxide" and "tetroxide" (author note c).
- **Memory aid (Revision 2):** "Ionic: name the charge if it can change. Covalent: count the atoms." It targets the genuine slip (a variable charge left out) and does not reject compositional names. Checked in "Memory aid check".

(a) Copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O, is a red to red-brown powder; copper(II) oxide, CuO, is a black powder (both standard laboratory reagents; CRC Handbook descriptions). Both are made of copper and oxygen only.
(b) Oxidation state: for a simple ion it equals the ion's charge. Oxidation numbers in molecules and polyatomic ions come in Module 3 (redox). Learner copy uses "the charge on the metal ion, also called its oxidation state".
(c) IUPAC Nomenclature of Inorganic Chemistry (Red Book, 2005), IR-5.2: multiplying prefixes are not elided except "monoxide"; "tetraoxide" is the strict form. NESA and most Australian texts use "tetroxide"; both are accepted. Screen uses the site's "tetroxide" with a small grey "(also tetraoxide)".
(d) Metals named as variable in learner copy: iron, copper, lead, tin. Single-charge metals named: sodium, magnesium, aluminium (and potassium, calcium in examples). Zinc and silver have one common charge; not raised.
(e) Common names (water, ammonia, methane) are IUPAC-accepted and not built from prefixes; one grey tag in scene 9 says "some molecules keep common names: water, ammonia". Hydrogen compounds such as HCl are named "hydrogen chloride" without prefixes by convention; not raised.
(g) Compositional names (Revision 2; IUPAC Red Book 2005, IR-5; https://iupac.qmul.ac.uk/BriefGuide/inorganic.html): names with multiplicative prefixes on ionic compounds (copper dichloride, iron trichloride, dipotassium oxide) are valid IUPAC names alongside Stock names (copper(II) chloride). Stock naming is the route taught here (root decision 37); the alternatives are named once in scene 11 as valid and are never crossed. Older oxidation-state names for molecular compounds (carbon(IV) oxide) are not shown.
(f) Pronunciations: "IUPAC" (EYE-you-pack); "Stock" (as the word); "copper two oxide", "copper one oxide", "iron three chloride", "iron two sulfate", "iron three sulfate", "lead four oxide" (the Roman numerals are spoken as numbers, the usual spoken form); "tetroxide" (teh-TROX-ide); "hexafluoride" (hex-a-FLOOR-ide); "pentachloride" (pen-ta-CLOR-ide).
